title: Cumulative distribution function
summary: The cdf is F(x)=P(X≤x). It is nondecreasing and right-continuous, with limits 0 and 1. Discrete cdfs jump by the point mass. Continuous cdfs have derivative equal to the density where the derivative exists. The quantile function inverts F.
intuition:
The cumulative distribution function records the probability sitting at or to the left of a point: $F(x)=P(X\le x)$. Every random variable has one, discrete or continuous. It starts near 0 far to the left and finishes near 1 far to the right. It never decreases. When it is flat, the variable puts no new probability there. When it jumps, the variable has an atom at that point.

For a discrete variable the jump at $x$ equals the point mass $P(X=x)$. The function is right-continuous: at a jump, $F(x)$ includes the atom, and the limit from the left does not. Reading the left limit as $F(x)$ drops the mass at $x$ and answers $P(X<x)$ instead of $P(X\le x)$.

For a continuous variable with a density, $F$ is continuous, so there are no jumps, and where the derivative exists

$$
f(x)=F'(x).
$$

The quantile of order $p$ runs this backwards. It is the left-inverse $F^{-1}(p)=\inf\{x:F(x)\ge p\}$. When $F$ is continuous and strictly increasing, that is the ordinary inverse: the point $q$ with $F(q)=p$. A median is the quantile of order $1/2$.

definitions.body: The function $F(x)=P(X\le x)$. The inequality is $\le$, so an atom at $x$ is included in $F(x)$.
The limit of $F$ from the right equals $F(x)$. For a discrete variable, the jump at $x$ is $F(x)$ minus the limit from the left, and that jump equals $P(X=x)$.
If $X$ is continuous with density $f$, then $f(x)=F'(x)$ at every $x$ where the derivative exists.
The quantile of order $p\in(0,1)$ is $F^{-1}(p)=\inf\{x:F(x)\ge p\}$. For a continuous strictly increasing cdf it is the ordinary inverse.

formulas.name: Definition and limits
formulas.note: The function is nondecreasing and right-continuous.

formulas.name: Jump and derivative
formulas.note: The jump formula is the discrete case. The derivative formula holds for a continuous law where $F'$ exists.

formulas.name: Quantile
formulas.note: When $F$ is continuous and strictly increasing, $F(F^{-1}(p))=p$.

properties: Every cdf satisfies $F(x)=P(X\le x)$, is nondecreasing and right-continuous, and has limits 0 at $-\infty$ and 1 at $+\infty$.
For a discrete variable, $F$ is a step function. The jump at $x$ equals the probability mass at $x$. Between atoms, $F$ is flat.
Right-continuity means $F(x)$ includes the mass at $x$. The left-hand limit equals $P(X<x)$.

For a continuous variable with density $f$, $F$ is continuous and $f=F'$ where the derivative exists. A corner, such as the endpoint of a uniform density, is a point where the derivative formula is not claimed.
The quantile function inverts $F$ from the left. The median is a 0.5-quantile. For a continuous strictly increasing $F$, it is the unique solution of $F(q)=1/2$.

examples.title: A discrete cdf with three atoms
steps: The cdf adds masses at or to the left of the argument. So $F(1)=0.2$ and $F(2)=0.2+0.5=0.7$.
There is no atom at 3, and nothing new between 2 and 4, so $F(3)=0.7$. Then $F(4)=0.7+0.3=1$.
The left limit at 2 is $F(1)=0.2$, because the function is flat on $[1,2)$. The jump is $0.7-0.2=0.5$, which equals $P(X=2)$. Right-continuity puts the value 0.7 at $x=2$ itself.
examples.answer: The values are $F(1)=0.2$, $F(2)=0.7$, $F(3)=0.7$, and the jump at 2 is $0.5$.

examples.title: A linear cdf and its quantile
examples.prompt: Let $F(x)=0$ for $x<1$, $F(x)=(x-1)/4$ for $1\le x\le 5$, and $F(x)=1$ for $x>5$. Find the density on $(1,5)$, the median, and the 0.75-quantile.
steps: On $(1,5)$ the derivative is $F'(x)=1/4$, so the density is the continuous uniform density of length 4. The derivative is not needed at the endpoints to identify the density in the open interval.
The median solves $(m-1)/4=1/2$, so $m-1=2$ and $m=3$. Check: $F(3)=(3-1)/4=1/2$.
examples.answer: The density on $(1,5)$ is $1/4$, the median is 3, and the 0.75-quantile is 4.

traps: Using a left-continuous step function. The cdf includes the atom: $F(x)=P(X\le x)$, so the value at a jump is the higher value. The left limit is $P(X<x)$.
Taking the jump to be something other than the point mass. In the three-atom example the jump at 2 is 0.5, not 0.7 and not 0.2.
Differentiating a discrete cdf and calling the result a density. A step function has derivative 0 away from the jumps and no ordinary derivative at a jump. The masses are the jumps, not a density.

Solving $F(q)=p$ from the wrong piece of a piecewise cdf, or reporting a negative root when the support is positive. For $F(x)=x^2$ on $[0,1]$, the median is $1/\sqrt{2}$, not $-1/\sqrt{2}$ and not $1/2$.
python:
from fractions import Fraction
f2 = Fraction(1, 5) + Fraction(1, 2)
assert f2 == Fraction(7, 10)
assert f2 + Fraction(3, 10) == 1
assert f2 - Fraction(1, 5) == Fraction(1, 2)
assert Fraction(3 - 1, 4) == Fraction(1, 2)
assert Fraction(4 - 1, 4) == Fraction(3, 4)
assert Fraction(1, 10) + Fraction(2, 5) == Fraction(1, 2)
print(float(f2), 3, 4)

questions.stem: A discrete random variable satisfies $P(X=0)=0.1$, $P(X=1)=0.4$, and $P(X=2)=0.5$. The cdf value $F(1)$ is
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, $0.5$.

The cdf adds every mass at or to the left of 1, so $F(1)=0.1+0.4=0.5$. Option B is only the jump at 1. Option C is $F(0)$. Option D is $F(1)+P(X=2)-0.1$, a scrambled total. Right-continuity includes the atom at 1.

questions.stem: The cdf is $F(x)=0$ for $x<0$, $F(x)=x^2$ for $0\le x\le 1$, and $F(x)=1$ for $x>1$. The median is
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, $1/\sqrt{2}$.

Solve $F(m)=1/2$ on $[0,1]$: $m^2=1/2$, and the nonnegative root is $1/\sqrt{2}$. Option B would be right for a uniform cdf on $[0,1]$, but here $F(1/2)=1/4$, which is option C and is not $1/2$. Option D is the right endpoint, where $F=1$.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true of every cumulative distribution function $F$?
options: The limit as $x\to -\infty$ is 0 and the limit as $x\to \infty$ is 1.
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and C**.

Those three properties are part of the definition of a cdf, together with $F(x)=P(X\le x)$. Option D is false. A discrete cdf jumps, and the jump equals the point mass. Continuity of $F$ is the special case with no atoms.

questions.stem: The cdf is $F(x)=0$ for $x<1$, $F(x)=(x-1)/4$ for $1\le x\le 5$, and $F(x)=1$ for $x>5$. Which of the following are true?
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and C**.

Substitute: $F(3)=(3-1)/4=1/2$. The equation $(q-1)/4=3/4$ gives $q=4$. Differentiating the linear piece gives the density $1/4$ on the open interval. Option D is false because $F(1)=(1-1)/4=0$. The line starts at 0 when $x=1$.

questions.stem: The cdf is $F(x)=0$ for $x<1$, $F(x)=(x-1)/4$ for $1\le x\le 5$, and $F(x)=1$ for $x>5$. Enter the quantile of order $0.75$.
questions.solution:
The answer is **4**.

Solve $(q-1)/4=0.75=3/4$. Then $q-1=3$ and $q=4$. The check is $F(4)=(4-1)/4=3/4$. The median of the same cdf is 3, which is the quantile of order $1/2$ and not the number asked for.
